answer.sourceLine: This is a genuine, word-for-word sentence from Thoreau’s ‘Walden’ (1854), opening the chapter “Where I Lived, and What I Lived For.” The popular wording matches the first edition exactly — a rare case where a line pinned to a fake-quote magnet is, in fact, authentic.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Walden; or, Life in the Woods
II — “Where I Lived, and What I Lived For”

source.excerpt: I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived. I did not wish to live what was not life, living is so dear; nor did I wish to practise resignation, unless it was quite necessary. I wanted to live deep and suck out all the marrow of life…
trail: The exact wording appears verbatim in the primary text of ‘Walden’ (1854) at Project Gutenberg ↗, in the chapter “Where I Lived, and What I Lived For.”
Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ attributes the line to ‘Walden’ (1854), citing it directly to the book.
The first edition was published by Ticknor and Fields, Boston, on 9 August 1854, per Wikipedia ↗ — long in the public domain.
source.excerptNote: The line opens the second chapter of ‘Walden’ — Thoreau’s answer to the question posed by the chapter’s own title.

author.name: Henry David Thoreau
author.heading: About Henry David Thoreau
author.bio: Henry David Thoreau was an American writer, philosopher, and naturalist, and a leading figure of New England Transcendentalism alongside his mentor Ralph Waldo Emerson. From 1845 to 1847 he lived in a small cabin he built near Walden Pond in Concord, Massachusetts; the experiment became the basis for ‘Walden’ (1854), his meditation on simple, intentional living. He is also remembered for the essay ‘Civil Disobedience’ (1849).

misattribution.heading: A real quote — but watch the wording
misattribution.intro: Thoreau is one of the internet’s biggest magnets for fabricated quotes, so it’s worth stating plainly: this one is authentic. The traps here are mis-wording and conflation, not false authorship.

items.who: Paraphrases that drop or reshape words
items.why: The genuine line reads “to front only the essential facts of life” and “suck out all the marrow of life.” Popular renderings often trim these — e.g. the “suck the marrow out of life” paraphrase familiar from the film ‘Dead Poets Society’ — but the first-edition text ↗ is as quoted here.

This sentence is frequently blended with Thoreau’s separate line “go confidently in the direction of your dreams,” which appears later in ‘Walden’ and is itself commonly misquoted in the imperative mood ↗. They are two distinct passages.

misattribution.truthLine: The core sentence is genuinely Thoreau, verbatim from ‘Walden’ (1854), Chapter II — confirmed against the primary text ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Thoreau moved to Walden Pond in July 1845 to test a philosophy: that a person could strip life down to essentials and discover what living actually required. This sentence — opening the chapter “Where I Lived, and What I Lived For” — is the clearest statement of that aim, and it became a founding text of American nature writing and Transcendentalist thought.

The passage endures because it frames deliberateness as a moral act: to reach the end of life without having truly lived is, for Thoreau, the real failure. It has since been adopted by environmentalists, minimalists, and mindfulness practitioners alike.
